entities.name: James of Viterbo
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
James of Viterbo, born Giacomo Capocci, was a pivotal Italian Scholastic theologian and Augustinian friar whose intellectual contributions significantly shaped medieval political thought and the articulation of papal authority. Flourishing in the late 13th and early 14th centuries, a period marked by intense ecclesiastical and temporal power struggles, James rose through the ranks of the Augustinian Order to become its provincial prior for Tuscany before ascending to the prestigious Chair of Theology at the University of Paris. His career culminated in his appointment as Archbishop of Naples in 1302, a role he held until his death in 1308.

His most celebrated work, *De regimine christiana* (On Christian Government), composed around 1301-1302, stands as a foundational text in the development of hierocratic political theology. In this treatise, James of Viterbo meticulously argued for the Pope's direct temporal authority over all secular rulers, asserting that all earthly power derives from and is ultimately subordinate to the spiritual authority of the Roman Pontiff. This bold defense of papal supremacy, drawing heavily on Aristotelian philosophy and Augustinian theological principles, directly addressed the burgeoning conflicts between King Philip IV of France and Pope Boniface VIII, providing a sophisticated intellectual framework for the papal cause.

The legacy of James of Viterbo extends beyond his immediate polemical context. His systematic approach to defining the nature of the Church, the role of the papacy, and the relationship between spiritual and temporal powers influenced subsequent generations of theologians and political theorists, including Giles of Rome and Augustinus Triumphus. His articulation of the Pope as the head of a universal Christian commonwealth, possessing both swords (spiritual and temporal) through divine mandate, became a cornerstone of high medieval hierocratic claims, echoing through the Avignon Papacy and beyond.
